pr.title: Record how a passkey registration picks its entry
pr.head: 5987946868f04d4cfc4230cf5359f731b6953f9f

summary: The passkeys plan designs a small Mac and iPhone app whose AutoFill extension creates passkeys and signs in with them, keeping each one as a passkey field on an entry in the multipass store. The plan is a draft, waiting on a prototype.

When a site asks the extension to register a new passkey, the extension has to choose which entry the passkey goes into. The owner already decided most of that in the plan's open questions, § 6 questions 7 to 9, but the design sections an implementer reads, § 2 and § 4, never said it. This pull request writes those decisions into the design, and records two newer rules in § 6 question 8.

• The same account registering again. When an entry's passkey has the same relying party ID and user handle as the new one, the new passkey replaces it in place, as WebAuthn has an authenticator do.
  • Any other registration. The passkey goes into the first of <rp id>, <rp id> <user name>, <rp id> <user name> 2, and so on, that holds no passkey. It joins that entry, beside its password and one-time password, when the entry exists, and creates it when it does not.
  • One passkey per entry. Each entry holds at most one passkey field, so each entry still describes one account, and every entry holds at least one of secret, otp, and passkey.
  • Checks to match. Three acceptance rows and two store-reader tests cover joining an existing entry, a second account's entry, and the same account registering again.
The plan stays draft. The first review's finding, that re-registering an account split it across entries, is fixed at this head, and the review signed the head off.

cards.title: Terms on this page
cards.html:
• Relying party ID (rp ID): the domain a passkey belongs to, such as github.com. The system checks it against the page.
  • User handle: the opaque account ID the site sends when it registers a passkey, stored as the field's user part. It differs between two accounts on one site.
  • User name: the readable account name the site sends, such as octocat.
  • Entry: one named record in the store, holding a password, a one-time password, a passkey, or several of them.

cards.title: Related plans
cards.html:
• Websites (ready, not built) adds a website field in format 4 and moves the passkey field to format 5 when it ships. This plan still says format 4, which matches that order.
  • Mergeable store (completed) merges whole entries, newest wins, and its history keeps no passkey, so a replaced passkey is gone for good, and two devices that register on the same site while one is offline keep only the newer passkey, as § 2.4 says.
  • Session unlock (completed): the extension opens the store itself and never asks the session agent.

cards.title: Review history
cards.html:
• ffebbc7: changes requested. Registering the same account again put the live passkey in a second entry, and a third registration had no defined entry.
  • cad3a27: clean. Step 5 replaces the same account's passkey by user handle and numbers later entries. Two follow-ups stay with the owner: picking the entry by website lines, and skipping an entry whose username names another account.
  • 9335383: clean. § 6 question 8 now records the replacement and numbered-name rules. One suggestion: say there that only an account whose <rp id> <user name> already holds a passkey takes a numbered name.
  • 5987946: clean, incremental. Question 8 now says exactly that, and the two follow-ups still stay with the owner.

groups.title: The passkeys plan
groups.kicker: Step 5 of § 2.1, § 2.2, the § 2.5 file table, § 4's rows and tests, and § 6 question 8
intro: Every change is in the one plan file. Read step 5 of § 2.1 first: it is the rule an implementer would follow, in order, when a site registers a passkey. § 2.2 then gives the store's side of it, at most one passkey field per entry, § 2.5 names the library calls the rule needs, § 4 adds the checks that prove it, and § 6 question 8 records the decision.

files.note: The plan: the registration rule in § 2.1 step 5, the one-passkey rule in § 2.2, and matching rows in § 2.5 and § 4.

checks.text: § 2.1 step 5: the replacement keys on the relying party ID and the user handle, which differs between accounts, so a second account's registration never overwrites the first one's passkey, and every later registration has a defined entry. Checked by walking the rule for a re-registration of octocat, a second account octocat-work, and a reused user name.

§ 2.2: an entry's name is the only key the rule uses besides the passkey itself. The rule neither reads the websites plan's website lines nor compares an entry's username, so a passkey can join an entry that describes another account. The review left both as follow-ups for the owner.
§ 2.5: the src/ffi.rs row now names every call step 5 needs: finding an entry by name, adding a passkey field to an existing entry, and replacing an entry's passkey.

§ 2.5: the src/store.rs row still names format 4, which matches the websites plan's § 2.4. That plan takes format 4 when it is built and moves this plan to format 5 then. Checked by reading both plans and AGENTS.md at the base.
§ 4: the new row checks the replacement end to end: after you remove the passkey on the site, registering the same account again leaves one entry, and the sign-in works.

§ 6 question 8: records step 5's replacement and numbered names. Another account gets the plain <rp id> <user name> entry, and only when that entry already holds a passkey does it take a numbered name, where a name is free when its entry holds no passkey. This agrees with step 5.
